### Las Terrenas – a resort village in the Dominican Republic

Las Terrenas is an idyllic resort village on the Samaná Peninsula. If you enjoy peaceful holidays away from the crowds, Las Terrenas is the place to go, surrounded by lush tropical nature. Those who prefer lively evenings will find plenty to do as well: after dark, numerous bars, nightclubs and discos open their doors.

Las Terrenas is known for its beaches. The almost two-kilometre-long Playa Las Terrenas is very clean, safe and shady, with a string of seaside restaurants where you can try an unusual local dish: grilled fish with coconut.

## Holidays in Las Terrenas

### The beautiful beaches of Las Terrenas!

Playa Cacao lies west of town and offers a wider range of beach activities. Playa Bonita is a broad stretch of fine sand fringed by coconut palms, with cottages and bungalows tucked beneath them. Playa Las Ballenas is popular with divers: coral colonies grow in its coastal waters, while a little farther offshore lies a tiny archipelago of uninhabited islands. At Playa Cosón, you can enjoy complete seclusion: an azure ocean, green palms and hardly another soul in sight.

Lemaire Channel separates Booth Island from the coast of Graham Land. From the ship, you can see steep mountain slopes, snowy peaks and ice along the water's edge. The passage connects sections of an expedition route along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula.

The Belgian Antarctic Expedition first navigated the channel in 1898; it was named after explorer Charles Lemaire. Ice conditions change, so the captain decides whether to sail through. When navigation is possible, the ship continues towards Pléneau and Petermann islands.

The lagoons are seasonal. Water depth and available routes vary from month to month, so it is best to choose travel dates according to conditions in the park. Once there, you can plan the itinerary around walks among the dunes, swimming and visits to famous lagoons, including Lagoa Azul.

In 2024, Lençóis Maranhenses National Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

León Viejo offers a glimpse of Nicaragua in the first decades of Spanish colonisation. The town was founded in 1524; following natural disasters, its inhabitants relocated it in 1610. Today, its low walls and surviving foundations reveal the layout of the old settlement: where houses stood, how the streets ran and which buildings occupied the central positions.

The archaeological site lies near Puerto Momotombo, on the western shore of Lake Managua, opposite Momotombo Volcano. Here, the town's history meets a volcanic landscape. León Viejo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and makes an excellent complement to a walk around modern León: first you discover the city's origins, then its cathedral, museums and streets.
